newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: National stresses list vote in NZ election.
newsitem.headline: National stresses list vote in NZ election.

text.p: New Zealand's conservative National Party government released its campaign slogan on Monday, urging its supporters not to split their vote at the October 12 general election.
National has opted for "First tick National" as its theme to counter what Prime Minister Jim Bolger says is widespread confusion over the importance of the party vote.

Under the German-style mixed member proportional system adopted by New Zealand, people will have two votes; for a party and for a local constituency MP. But it is the first, party, vote which determines the overall make-up of parliament.
On current polling, the ruling National-United party coalition will fail to win a majority in parliament.

Bolger told a news conference National had opted not to have a "promise line" in its slogan because "there seemed little value in convincing the voters of our virtues if they don't clearly understand how to vote us in".
A poll released in this morning's "Dominion" newspaper showed 62 percent of those polled were still not aware of the importance of the party vote in deciding the government.
Awareness had improved only eight percentage points in two years despite an extensive education campaign by the Electoral Commission.

Pollster Stephen Mills of UMR-Insight, which conducted the poll, said both National and the opposition Labour Party were at risk from vote-splitting, and the country could get a government that was at odds with voters' intentions.
Bolger said many voters had been confused by publicity put out by free-market party ACT that a party vote cast for ACT was the best path to a National government.

ACT is drawing support at just below the five percent threshold at which parties qualify for party list seats and is seen as a natural supporter of a National-led government, although its leader, former Labour cabinet minister Richard Prebble, has ruled out a formal coalition.

Bolger said ACT's publicity was both self-serving and highly inaccurate, and that the publicity of the "secretive" organisation 'Vote', which was using the same "flawed logic", was also confusing the public.
The Vote group has refused to say who is funding it, but is also advocating vote-splitting.
Bolger said the "tick National first" slogan was not an abandonment of its "two ticks" campaign but a refinement of it.

National will be pushing the secondary theme of "so far, so near, so let's keep going forward" to highlight the achievements of the 1990-96 National government and stress the dangers of changing the government when "the best is yet to come", Bolger said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
